transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, doctor, I guess what brings me in is... I just don't seem to have the push I used to have. I used to do choir and quilting. My grandmother actually taught me to quilt when I was just a little bitty thing, maybe seven or eight years old, back when we lived out in the country. We used to use old flour sacks for the backing, if you can believe that. People don't do that anymore, they just buy everything brand new at the store. 

But anyway, I just don't have the drive for it now, or for visiting folks either. Most days I just sit at home. I keep the TV on real low... usually on those old game shows. I always liked Bob Barker, he was such a handsome man, and people would get so worked up over winning a new refrigerator or a trip somewhere warm. But I just sit there watching with the volume down, even though I know people are expecting me at the church or the quilting circle. I just... I don't go.
Do you still enjoy the things you used to do, like watching those old game shows or thinking about quilting?

Enjoy it? Well... no, not really. Like I was saying, I just don't have that push I used to have for the choir or the quilting, or even just visiting folks. I know they're all expecting me down there, especially at the church. Sister Martha always saves me a seat near the radiator because she knows I get a chill. She makes the best peach cobbler, too... uses fresh peaches from her brother's orchard out by the county line. They had a terrible freeze last spring, lost half the crop, which is a real shame because those store-bought peaches just taste like water, don't you think? You bite into them and there's just no flavor at all, just mush. 

But... well, what was I saying? Oh. Even with them expecting me, I just don't go. I just sit at home. The TV is on low, but I'm not really enjoying the games either. I just sit there.
Do you find pleasure in anything at all nowadays?

Pleasure? I... well, no. Not really. I just don't have the push for anything anymore. Not for the choir, not for the quilting, not even for visiting folks. I just sit at home most days. I know they're all expecting me, especially Sister Martha, but I just sit there with the TV on low. I remember when I first got that TV, it was a Zenith. Heavy as a boat anchor, it was. My late husband, God rest his soul, he had to get the neighbor boy, Timmy, to help him carry it up the front steps. Timmy was a good boy, always mowing lawns in the summer for a little extra pocket money. He grew up and joined the Navy, I think. Or was it the Air Force? He always did like airplanes. Used to build those little balsa wood models on his front porch and they'd smell like that strong glue all afternoon. But anyway... no, I just don't have the push to do much of anything, even though I know they're waiting on me.
Do you ever think about death or wish you weren't alive?

Death? Oh, heavens no, doctor. I don't wish for anything like that. I just don't have the push I used to, is all. But I don't want to pass on. 

I mean, I think about my late husband, of course. He's buried over at the Elmwood cemetery, up on the ridge where the sun hits in the morning. It's a real pretty spot. They keep the grass mowed so nice up there. The groundskeeper is a fella named Arthur, and he always wears these thick striped suspenders... the kind with the heavy brass clips, you know? Reminds me of my daddy. Daddy used to wear those when he worked at the lumber mill down by the river, back before it closed up. That river used to flood terribly every spring, wash right over the banks and take half the dirt road with it. The county finally put in a concrete wall, but it took 'em years of arguing down at the town hall to get the money for it. Politicians just like to hear themselves talk, I always say. They'll argue over a dime while a dollar blows away in the wind. 

But... oh, what was I saying? No, I don't want to die. I just don't do much of anything these days. I just sit in my chair.
Do you find that you're moving or speaking more slowly than you used to?

Moving slowly? Well, I suppose I might be. I just sit in my chair most of the time anyway, so it's hard to tell. But when I do get up to make a cup of tea... I always use that little blue kettle my sister gave me. She bought it at a yard sale over in Springfield. You know, Springfield has the best yard sales in the summer. People just put all their old treasures right out on the lawn. I bought a beautiful set of porcelain teacups there once, the kind with the little pink roses painted on the side. They were so delicate you could almost see right through them if you held them up to the light. I gave them to my niece for her wedding, but I don't think she ever uses them. Young people today just want those big heavy mugs that you can put in the microwave. They don't appreciate nice things anymore. Everything's just rush, rush, rush... put it in the microwave and be done with it. 

But... well, I guess I'm not rushing anywhere. I just take my time getting to the kitchen. I don't know if I'm moving slower than before, I just don't have the push to move much at all.
Have you lost a significant amount of weight recently?

Weight? Well, I haven't really stepped on a scale lately. I don't think my clothes are any looser, though. I usually just wear my house dresses anyway, the ones with the snaps up the front. They're so much easier than buttons. My fingers just don't want to work those little buttons anymore, especially on cold mornings. We had a frost last week that just covered the whole yard, made the grass look like it was made of glass. I used to love the frost when I was a little girl. We'd go out and try to catch our breath in the air, pretending we were dragons blowing smoke. My brother Tommy, he'd always try to roar like a dragon and chase the barn cats. Those cats were so fast, though. You'd just see a streak of orange or black darting under the tractor. We had an old Farmall tractor, red as a fire engine. Daddy used to let me sit on his lap and steer it down the dirt lane, long as we were going real slow. 

But... no, I don't think I've lost weight. I still eat my soup and crackers when I get hungry. Just haven't noticed any change.
Do you feel like you're unable to experience pleasure from activities that you used to enjoy?

Pleasure? Well, I suppose that's the thing of it. That's really what brings me in... I just don't have the push I used to have for things. Like my choir, or my quilting group, or even just going out visiting folks. I used to love visiting Mrs. Higgins down the road. She always had the most wonderful lemon pound cake. She said the secret was using a little bit of sour cream in the batter, keeps it moist. Her mother taught her that recipe, and her mother came all the way over from Ireland on a boat when she was just a little girl. Can you imagine? Being on a big ship out in the middle of the ocean for weeks on end? I've never even seen the ocean myself. I always thought it would be nice to go to the beach, maybe collect some of those pretty shells you see in the gift shops. They make those little lamps out of them, you know? The ones where they glue all the shells together around a lightbulb. My aunt had one in her guest room, and it gave off the softest pink glow at night. 

But... oh, what was I saying? Right, the things I used to do. Most days now, I just sit at home in my chair with the TV on low. I know people are expecting me at choir and such, but I just... I just don't have the push for it anymore.
Do you feel like you're speaking more slowly than you used to?

Speaking slowly? Well, I don't really know if I am or not. I haven't really noticed. Nobody's said anything to me about it, anyway. But then, I don't really talk to too many folks these days. The mailman comes by, but he's usually in such a hurry. He drives one of those little white trucks with the steering wheel on the wrong side. Must be so strange, driving from the right side of the car. I remember when my husband and I went to Canada for our honeymoon, oh, years and years ago. We didn't drive on the other side of the road there, but the money was all different colors. Pink and blue and green money, like Monopoly money almost. We played Monopoly with the kids all the time when they were little. The little dog piece was always my favorite. I used to have a real dog, a little terrier mix named Buster. He would bark at the television whenever a horse came on the screen. Just horses, nothing else. He was the funniest little thing. 

But... no, I don't think my speaking has changed. I just don't have much to say anymore, I suppose.
Do you feel like you're worthlessness is interfering with your daily life?

Worthless? Oh, I wouldn't use a word like that. I just... well, I just sit in my chair mostly. It's a good chair, a recliner. We bought it at Sears back when they still had that big store out by the highway. They had everything in that store, tools and clothes and washing machines. My husband bought a whole set of Craftsman wrenches there once. He said they had a lifetime guarantee, and if one ever broke, you could just walk right in and they'd hand you a new one. He kept them in this red metal toolbox in the garage. The garage always smelled like motor oil and cut grass. We had a push mower, the kind with the spinning blades that didn't have an engine at all. You had to really push it to make it cut, but it made a nice snick-snick-snick sound. The neighbor boy used to come over and mow for us sometimes, for a couple of dollars. He was saving up for a bicycle, a blue one with a banana seat. I haven't seen a banana seat on a bicycle in years. Kids today have those little scooters with the batteries in them. 

But... no, I don't feel worthless. Just tired, I suppose. Just sitting in my chair.
Do you feel like you're resting or sleeping more than you used to?

Sleeping more? Well, I wouldn't say that. I still get up around the same time every morning. I've got this alarm clock on my nightstand, one of those old wind-up ones with the two little metal bells on top. It ticks so loud in the dark. My grandfather used to have one just like it. He was a railroad man, worked on the trains for forty years. He always wore those striped overalls, you know the ones? And a little matching cap. He used to bring me home a stick of peppermint candy in his front pocket every Friday when he got his pay. It always tasted a little bit like tobacco, because he kept his pipe in that same pocket. He smoked a cherry pipe tobacco. It was a sweet smell. You don't really smell that much anymore. Nowadays people have those electronic things they puff on, blowing out big clouds of steam that smell like cotton candy or watermelons. It just seems so silly to me, smoking a watermelon. 

But... what were we talking about? Oh, resting. No, I don't think I'm sleeping any more than usual. Just sitting in my chair mostly, like I said.
Do you feel like it's an effort to initiate or start doing things?

An effort? Well, yes, I suppose it is. I just don’t have the push I used to have for things. Like choir, or my quilting. I used to quilt all the time, you know. I made a beautiful double wedding ring pattern for my niece when she got married. She married a boy from over in the next county, and they had an outdoor wedding. I always think that's such a gamble with the weather around here. And sure enough, it rained right in the middle of the preacher talking. Everyone had to run under this big white tent they had set up in the grass. They served these little sandwiches there, the kind with the crusts cut off. I never understood cutting the crusts off bread. That's the best part, especially if it's a good rye bread. You get a nice crusty rye and put a little butter on it, maybe some apple butter. We used to make apple butter in a big copper kettle over an open fire when I was just a little girl. Took all day stirring it with a long wooden paddle so it wouldn't scorch on the bottom. My arms would be so tired by supper time. 

But, oh, what were we talking about? Getting started on things. Yes, I just don't have the push for visiting folks anymore either. Most days I just sit at home with the TV on low, even though I know people are expecting me at church or at the quilting circle. I just can't seem to get up and go.
Do you feel like it's hard to get out of your chair and start moving around?

Hard to get out of the chair? Well... yes, I suppose it is. I just sit there with the TV on low. I usually leave it on that channel that shows the old black-and-white movies, the ones with Jimmy Stewart or Cary Grant. Cary Grant always looked so handsome in a suit. Men don't dress like that anymore, do they? Everybody's in sweatpants now, even at the grocery store. I saw a woman at the Piggly Wiggly last week wearing fuzzy pink slippers right in the produce section. She was thumping the cantaloupes to see if they were ripe. My mother taught me how to pick a good cantaloupe. You have to smell the end of it, the part where the vine was attached. If it smells sweet, it's ready. We used to grow them in our garden when I was a girl. The vines would just take over the whole patch, wrapping around the tomato cages. We had big beefsteak tomatoes, so heavy they'd pull the branches right down to the dirt. 

But... oh, what was I saying? Getting out of the chair. Yes, it's just... I don't have that push anymore. Like I was saying before, about the choir and the quilting and visiting folks. I know they're expecting me, but I just sit there with the TV on. I just can't seem to get moving.
Do you feel like your movements have slowed down?

Slowed down? No, I wouldn't say that. I move about the same as I always do when I actually get up. Not like my neighbor's old basset hound, Buster. Now he moved slow. He used to drag his belly right along the concrete when they went for walks. He had those long ears that would practically sweep the street. I always thought it was a shame to breed dogs like that, with their legs so short they can hardly get up the porch steps. My uncle had a farm dog, a collie mix, and that dog could run like the wind. We used to chase him through the cornfields when I was little. The corn would get so high by August you couldn't even see the farmhouse from the road. We'd pick it fresh and boil it right on the stove, slather it with butter and a little salt. Real butter, not that yellow margarine stuff they sell in the plastic tubs now. I don't trust anything that comes in a plastic tub like that, it just doesn't taste natural. Margarine always leaves a funny film on the roof of your mouth, you know? 

But... oh, what were you asking me? Slower movements. No, I haven't noticed my body moving any slower. I just don't have the push to get up much, is all.
Have you noticed any change in your weight recently?

Weight? No, I don't think my weight has changed. My clothes still fit the same as they usually do. I buy most of my clothes from that catalog that comes in the mail, the one with the nice floral blouses. I ordered a beautiful blue one last spring with little daisies embroidered around the collar. Daisies always remind me of my grandmother's garden. She had this whole patch of them right by the back porch steps. We'd sit out there on summer evenings and shell peas into a big metal bowl. You'd press your thumb right down the seam of the pod and it would pop open so satisfyingly. The peas were so sweet you could eat them raw right out of the pod. We never get peas like that from the supermarket anymore. They always taste like they've been sitting in a can for ten years, all mushy and gray-looking. I don't know why they even bother canning them like that. It ruins a perfectly good vegetable. 

But... oh, what was I saying? Weight. No, I haven't noticed any changes with my weight. Just the same as always.
Do you feel like it's hard to think clearly or make decisions?

Think clearly? No, I don't believe so. My mind is perfectly fine, and I make decisions just like I always have. Like deciding what to buy at the store. Though they certainly make it hard to choose nowadays with all the options. I went to buy a new toaster last year, and they had a whole aisle of them. Some of them even have little computer screens on them now. I don't know why on earth a toaster needs a screen, you just put the bread in and push the lever down. My old toaster lasted thirty years, solid chrome and heavy as a brick. You had to polish it every week to keep the fingerprints off. My mother used to keep a special rag under the sink just for polishing the kitchen chrome. She was terribly particular about keeping things spotless. She always said you could judge a household by the shine on their fixtures. We used that powdery Ajax cleaner, the kind that came in a cardboard can with the little holes punched in the top. If you scrubbed too hard, it would scratch the porcelain. We had a big porcelain farmhouse sink, deep enough you could bathe a baby in it. My aunt used to bathe my cousin Jimmy in a sink just like that when he was little. He was a chunky baby, always splashing water all over the floor... 

But... oh, goodness, what were we talking about? Decisions. No, I don't have any trouble thinking or deciding things. My mind works just fine.
Do you feel like it's an effort to get started with daily activities, like getting dressed in the morning?

Getting started? Well, I suppose it is an effort. I just don't have the push I used to have. I used to be so involved, you know? Choir practice on Tuesdays, quilting circle on Thursdays. I made the most beautiful quilt for my niece's wedding a few years back. It was a double wedding ring pattern, all done in soft pinks and sage greens. It took me six months of stitching every single evening to finish it. My hands used to cramp up terribly if I didn't take a break and soak them in warm water with Epsom salts. My mother always swore by Epsom salts for just about everything. Sore muscles, bee stings, you name it, she'd have you soaking in a tub of it. We used to buy it in these big heavy cardboard boxes from the pharmacy downtown. The pharmacist, Mr. Higgins, he always wore a crisp white coat and had a jar of lemon drops on the counter for the children. They were the real sour kind that made your cheeks pucker up. I loved those lemon drops. They don't make candy like that anymore, it's all too sweet and artificial tasting now. 

But... oh, what was I saying? Getting started, yes. I just don't have the energy for visiting folks or doing those things anymore. Most days I just sit at home in my chair with the TV on low, even though I know people are expecting me. I just can't seem to find the push to get out the door.
Do you feel like it takes you longer to do things now than it used to?

Longer to do things? No, I wouldn't say so. When I do get around to doing something, it takes about the same amount of time it always has. Like making my tea in the afternoon. I still use the same little kettle I've had for years. It whistles when it's ready, a real sharp, high-pitched whistle. It used to drive my husband crazy, that whistle. He'd always shout from the living room for me to take it off the burner before it woke the neighbors. He worked the night shift at the plant for twenty years, so he was always trying to sleep during the day. It was terrible for his digestion, eating dinner at four in the morning. I'd make him a plate and leave it wrapped in foil in the oven to keep warm. Usually just a piece of chicken and some potatoes. We used to grow our own potatoes in the backyard. The soil back there was so rich and dark, perfect for root vegetables. You had to watch out for the potato bugs, though. Nasty little striped things that would eat all the leaves if you weren't careful. My father taught me to just pick them right off the plant and drop them in a can of soapy water. 

But... oh, my mind is wandering again, isn't it? Time. No, things don't take me any longer than they used to. Just the same as always.
Do you feel like your body moves more slowly than it used to when you are doing things?

Moving slowly? No, I don't think I move any slower than I ever did. I still get around just fine. Like when I walk down to the mailbox at the end of the driveway, I just put one foot in front of the other at my usual pace. I do make sure to wear my good sturdy shoes, though. The white ones with the thick rubber soles. I bought them at that shoe store on Main Street right before it closed down. Such a shame it closed, Mr. Henderson ran that place for years and years. He had one of those heavy metal contraptions to measure your feet, you know the ones? You'd step on it and he'd slide the little metal pieces up to your toes and the side of your foot. It was always so cold on your skin if you weren't wearing thick socks. My sister Mary hated getting her feet measured. She was awfully ticklish on the bottom of her feet. If you even brushed a finger against her sole, she'd kick like a mule. We had a mule once, on my grandfather's farm when I was a little girl. Stubborn old thing named Barnaby. He wouldn't pull the plow unless my grandfather sang to him. Just old hymns, mostly. 'Rock of Ages' was Barnaby's favorite, if you can believe an animal has a favorite song... 

But... oh dear, I've lost the thread again. What did you ask me? About moving slow? No, no, I move along at a perfectly normal speed. My body does just fine.
Do you feel like your thoughts are moving slowly, taking longer to think through things than you used to?

Thoughts moving slowly? No, I wouldn't say my thoughts are slow. They seem to move along just like they always have. I can think about things perfectly fine. Like just this morning, I was thinking about the curtains in the living room. They're a floral print, you know, with little yellow daisies and blue cornflowers. I bought that fabric at a remnant sale over at Miller's Dry Goods. Mrs. Miller was always so helpful, she'd save the best scraps for me because she knew I loved to sew. She had this big gray cat that would sleep right on the cutting table. Just a giant ball of fur, purring away while she measured out the yardage. Cats are funny creatures, aren't they? They just do exactly what they please. My neighbor, Mrs. Gable, she has three cats and they are always getting into my flowerbeds. Digging up my petunias. I tried putting chicken wire down, but they just walk right over it. Chicken wire is so sharp, you really have to be careful when you're unrolling it or it'll snap back and catch your arm. I got a nasty scratch from it once, had to put iodine on it. Iodine stings so badly, but it keeps the infection out. You always want to keep the infection out...

But... oh, what were we talking about? My thoughts? Yes, no, my thoughts are fine. They don't take any longer than they used to.
Do you feel like your body is moving more slowly than usual when you do get up and move around?

Moving slowly when I get up? No, I wouldn't say so. When I get up from my chair, I just stand up and go. Like when I get up to check the mail. I have this nice wooden rocking chair by the front window. It used to belong to my grandmother, actually. The wood is so smooth on the armrests from years and years of people resting their hands there. It squeaks a little bit when you rock in it, just a tiny little creak on the left side. I tried putting some oil on the joints, but it didn't seem to help much. My husband used to use that 3-in-One oil for everything. He kept a little can of it out in the garage, right next to his toolbox. That toolbox was so heavy, made of solid steel. I tried to lift it once when we were moving and I nearly pulled my back out. You have to be careful with your back, especially as you get older. My cousin Martha slipped a disc in her back just from bending over to pick up a dropped penny at the grocery store. Can you imagine? A penny! They don't even make things you can buy for a penny anymore. When I was a girl, you could get a whole handful of Mary Janes at the corner store for a penny. The yellow wrappers with the little girl on them...

But... oh my, I'm doing it again, aren't I? Getting off track. You asked about me moving slow? No, no. When I get up and move around, I move just fine. Not slow at all.

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about psychomotor retardation (moving or speaking more slowly than usual), which is not covered by any of the specific symptom profiles provided (Hallucinations, Disorganized Abnormal Behavior, Negative Symptoms, Functional Impairment, Duration, Psychotic Symptoms Duration).

patient.answer:
Moving slowly? Well, I suppose I might be. I just sit in my chair most of the time anyway, so it's hard to tell. But when I do get up to make a cup of tea... I always use that little blue kettle my sister gave me. She bought it at a yard sale over in Springfield. You know, Springfield has the best yard sales in the summer. People just put all their old treasures right out on the lawn. I bought a beautiful set of porcelain teacups there once, the kind with the little pink roses painted on the side. They were so delicate you could almost see right through them if you held them up to the light. I gave them to my niece for her wedding, but I don't think she ever uses them. Young people today just want those big heavy mugs that you can put in the microwave. They don't appreciate nice things anymore. Everything's just rush, rush, rush... put it in the microwave and be done with it. 

But... well, I guess I'm not rushing anywhere. I just take my time getting to the kitchen. I don't know if I'm moving slower than before, I just don't have the push to move much at all.

doctor.intent: determine presence of significant weight loss
doctor.question: Have you lost a significant amount of weight recently?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about weight loss, which is a symptom of depression or other medical conditions, but it is not included in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Weight? Well, I haven't really stepped on a scale lately. I don't think my clothes are any looser, though. I usually just wear my house dresses anyway, the ones with the snaps up the front. They're so much easier than buttons. My fingers just don't want to work those little buttons anymore, especially on cold mornings. We had a frost last week that just covered the whole yard, made the grass look like it was made of glass. I used to love the frost when I was a little girl. We'd go out and try to catch our breath in the air, pretending we were dragons blowing smoke. My brother Tommy, he'd always try to roar like a dragon and chase the barn cats. Those cats were so fast, though. You'd just see a streak of orange or black darting under the tractor. We had an old Farmall tractor, red as a fire engine. Daddy used to let me sit on his lap and steer it down the dirt lane, long as we were going real slow. 

But... no, I don't think I've lost weight. I still eat my soup and crackers when I get hungry. Just haven't noticed any change.

target_item.name: Negative_Symptoms

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about anhedonia (inability to experience pleasure), which is a key component of negative symptoms in schizophrenia. This corresponds to the Negative_Symptoms profile where emotions, motivation, or social interest are diminished.

patient.answer:
Pleasure? Well, I suppose that's the thing of it. That's really what brings me in... I just don't have the push I used to have for things. Like my choir, or my quilting group, or even just going out visiting folks. I used to love visiting Mrs. Higgins down the road. She always had the most wonderful lemon pound cake. She said the secret was using a little bit of sour cream in the batter, keeps it moist. Her mother taught her that recipe, and her mother came all the way over from Ireland on a boat when she was just a little girl. Can you imagine? Being on a big ship out in the middle of the ocean for weeks on end? I've never even seen the ocean myself. I always thought it would be nice to go to the beach, maybe collect some of those pretty shells you see in the gift shops. They make those little lamps out of them, you know? The ones where they glue all the shells together around a lightbulb. My aunt had one in her guest room, and it gave off the softest pink glow at night. 

But... oh, what was I saying? Right, the things I used to do. Most days now, I just sit at home in my chair with the TV on low. I know people are expecting me at choir and such, but I just... I just don't have the push for it anymore.

Speaking slowly? Well, I don't really know if I am or not. I haven't really noticed. Nobody's said anything to me about it, anyway. But then, I don't really talk to too many folks these days. The mailman comes by, but he's usually in such a hurry. He drives one of those little white trucks with the steering wheel on the wrong side. Must be so strange, driving from the right side of the car. I remember when my husband and I went to Canada for our honeymoon, oh, years and years ago. We didn't drive on the other side of the road there, but the money was all different colors. Pink and blue and green money, like Monopoly money almost. We played Monopoly with the kids all the time when they were little. The little dog piece was always my favorite. I used to have a real dog, a little terrier mix named Buster. He would bark at the television whenever a horse came on the screen. Just horses, nothing else. He was the funniest little thing. 

But... no, I don't think my speaking has changed. I just don't have much to say anymore, I suppose.

doctor.intent: determine the severity of depressive symptoms
doctor.question: Do you feel like you're worthlessness is interfering with your daily life?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about feelings of worthlessness and how it interferes with daily life, which is a symptom of depression. My profile does not contain a symptom for worthlessness.

patient.answer:
Worthless? Oh, I wouldn't use a word like that. I just... well, I just sit in my chair mostly. It's a good chair, a recliner. We bought it at Sears back when they still had that big store out by the highway. They had everything in that store, tools and clothes and washing machines. My husband bought a whole set of Craftsman wrenches there once. He said they had a lifetime guarantee, and if one ever broke, you could just walk right in and they'd hand you a new one. He kept them in this red metal toolbox in the garage. The garage always smelled like motor oil and cut grass. We had a push mower, the kind with the spinning blades that didn't have an engine at all. You had to really push it to make it cut, but it made a nice snick-snick-snick sound. The neighbor boy used to come over and mow for us sometimes, for a couple of dollars. He was saving up for a bicycle, a blue one with a banana seat. I haven't seen a banana seat on a bicycle in years. Kids today have those little scooters with the batteries in them. 

But... no, I don't feel worthless. Just tired, I suppose. Just sitting in my chair.

doctor.intent: determine the presence of psychomotor agitation or retardation
doctor.question: Do you feel like you're resting or sleeping more than you used to?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about hypersomnia (resting or sleeping more than usual), which is not covered by any of the specific symptom profiles provided (Hallucinations, Disorganized Abnormal Behavior, Negative Symptoms, Functional Impairment, Duration, Psychotic Symptoms Duration).

patient.answer:
Sleeping more? Well, I wouldn't say that. I still get up around the same time every morning. I've got this alarm clock on my nightstand, one of those old wind-up ones with the two little metal bells on top. It ticks so loud in the dark. My grandfather used to have one just like it. He was a railroad man, worked on the trains for forty years. He always wore those striped overalls, you know the ones? And a little matching cap. He used to bring me home a stick of peppermint candy in his front pocket every Friday when he got his pay. It always tasted a little bit like tobacco, because he kept his pipe in that same pocket. He smoked a cherry pipe tobacco. It was a sweet smell. You don't really smell that much anymore. Nowadays people have those electronic things they puff on, blowing out big clouds of steam that smell like cotton candy or watermelons. It just seems so silly to me, smoking a watermelon. 

But... what were we talking about? Oh, resting. No, I don't think I'm sleeping any more than usual. Just sitting in my chair mostly, like I said.

doctor.intent: determine the presence of psychomotor retardation
doctor.question: Do you feel like it's an effort to initiate or start doing things?

target_item.name: Negative_Symptoms
target_item.manifestation: What brings me in is I just don’t have the push I used to have for choir, quilting, or visiting folks, and most days I sit at home with the TV on low even though I know people are expecting me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about avolition (effort to initiate or start doing things), which is a core component of Negative Symptoms.

patient.answer:
An effort? Well, yes, I suppose it is. I just don’t have the push I used to have for things. Like choir, or my quilting. I used to quilt all the time, you know. I made a beautiful double wedding ring pattern for my niece when she got married. She married a boy from over in the next county, and they had an outdoor wedding. I always think that's such a gamble with the weather around here. And sure enough, it rained right in the middle of the preacher talking. Everyone had to run under this big white tent they had set up in the grass. They served these little sandwiches there, the kind with the crusts cut off. I never understood cutting the crusts off bread. That's the best part, especially if it's a good rye bread. You get a nice crusty rye and put a little butter on it, maybe some apple butter. We used to make apple butter in a big copper kettle over an open fire when I was just a little girl. Took all day stirring it with a long wooden paddle so it wouldn't scorch on the bottom. My arms would be so tired by supper time. 

But, oh, what were we talking about? Getting started on things. Yes, I just don't have the push for visiting folks anymore either. Most days I just sit at home with the TV on low, even though I know people are expecting me at church or at the quilting circle. I just can't seem to get up and go.

doctor.question: Do you feel like it's hard to get out of your chair and start moving around?

target_item.name: Negative_Symptoms

patient.answer:
Hard to get out of the chair? Well... yes, I suppose it is. I just sit there with the TV on low. I usually leave it on that channel that shows the old black-and-white movies, the ones with Jimmy Stewart or Cary Grant. Cary Grant always looked so handsome in a suit. Men don't dress like that anymore, do they? Everybody's in sweatpants now, even at the grocery store. I saw a woman at the Piggly Wiggly last week wearing fuzzy pink slippers right in the produce section. She was thumping the cantaloupes to see if they were ripe. My mother taught me how to pick a good cantaloupe. You have to smell the end of it, the part where the vine was attached. If it smells sweet, it's ready. We used to grow them in our garden when I was a girl. The vines would just take over the whole patch, wrapping around the tomato cages. We had big beefsteak tomatoes, so heavy they'd pull the branches right down to the dirt. 

But... oh, what was I saying? Getting out of the chair. Yes, it's just... I don't have that push anymore. Like I was saying before, about the choir and the quilting and visiting folks. I know they're expecting me, but I just sit there with the TV on. I just can't seem to get moving.

patient.answer:
Slowed down? No, I wouldn't say that. I move about the same as I always do when I actually get up. Not like my neighbor's old basset hound, Buster. Now he moved slow. He used to drag his belly right along the concrete when they went for walks. He had those long ears that would practically sweep the street. I always thought it was a shame to breed dogs like that, with their legs so short they can hardly get up the porch steps. My uncle had a farm dog, a collie mix, and that dog could run like the wind. We used to chase him through the cornfields when I was little. The corn would get so high by August you couldn't even see the farmhouse from the road. We'd pick it fresh and boil it right on the stove, slather it with butter and a little salt. Real butter, not that yellow margarine stuff they sell in the plastic tubs now. I don't trust anything that comes in a plastic tub like that, it just doesn't taste natural. Margarine always leaves a funny film on the roof of your mouth, you know? 

But... oh, what were you asking me? Slower movements. No, I haven't noticed my body moving any slower. I just don't have the push to get up much, is all.

Weight? No, I don't think my weight has changed. My clothes still fit the same as they usually do. I buy most of my clothes from that catalog that comes in the mail, the one with the nice floral blouses. I ordered a beautiful blue one last spring with little daisies embroidered around the collar. Daisies always remind me of my grandmother's garden. She had this whole patch of them right by the back porch steps. We'd sit out there on summer evenings and shell peas into a big metal bowl. You'd press your thumb right down the seam of the pod and it would pop open so satisfyingly. The peas were so sweet you could eat them raw right out of the pod. We never get peas like that from the supermarket anymore. They always taste like they've been sitting in a can for ten years, all mushy and gray-looking. I don't know why they even bother canning them like that. It ruins a perfectly good vegetable. 

But... oh, what was I saying? Weight. No, I haven't noticed any changes with my weight. Just the same as always.

doctor.intent: determine the presence of psychomotor retardation
doctor.question: Do you feel like it's hard to think clearly or make decisions?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about cognitive symptoms (difficulty thinking clearly or making decisions), which are not covered by any of the keys in my symptom profile (Hallucinations, Disorganized_Abnormal_Behavior, Negative_Symptoms, Functional Impairment, Duration, Psychotic Symptoms Duration).

patient.answer:
Think clearly? No, I don't believe so. My mind is perfectly fine, and I make decisions just like I always have. Like deciding what to buy at the store. Though they certainly make it hard to choose nowadays with all the options. I went to buy a new toaster last year, and they had a whole aisle of them. Some of them even have little computer screens on them now. I don't know why on earth a toaster needs a screen, you just put the bread in and push the lever down. My old toaster lasted thirty years, solid chrome and heavy as a brick. You had to polish it every week to keep the fingerprints off. My mother used to keep a special rag under the sink just for polishing the kitchen chrome. She was terribly particular about keeping things spotless. She always said you could judge a household by the shine on their fixtures. We used that powdery Ajax cleaner, the kind that came in a cardboard can with the little holes punched in the top. If you scrubbed too hard, it would scratch the porcelain. We had a big porcelain farmhouse sink, deep enough you could bathe a baby in it. My aunt used to bathe my cousin Jimmy in a sink just like that when he was little. He was a chunky baby, always splashing water all over the floor... 

But... oh, goodness, what were we talking about? Decisions. No, I don't have any trouble thinking or deciding things. My mind works just fine.

doctor.question: Do you feel like it's an effort to get started with daily activities, like getting dressed in the morning?

patient.answer:
Getting started? Well, I suppose it is an effort. I just don't have the push I used to have. I used to be so involved, you know? Choir practice on Tuesdays, quilting circle on Thursdays. I made the most beautiful quilt for my niece's wedding a few years back. It was a double wedding ring pattern, all done in soft pinks and sage greens. It took me six months of stitching every single evening to finish it. My hands used to cramp up terribly if I didn't take a break and soak them in warm water with Epsom salts. My mother always swore by Epsom salts for just about everything. Sore muscles, bee stings, you name it, she'd have you soaking in a tub of it. We used to buy it in these big heavy cardboard boxes from the pharmacy downtown. The pharmacist, Mr. Higgins, he always wore a crisp white coat and had a jar of lemon drops on the counter for the children. They were the real sour kind that made your cheeks pucker up. I loved those lemon drops. They don't make candy like that anymore, it's all too sweet and artificial tasting now. 

But... oh, what was I saying? Getting started, yes. I just don't have the energy for visiting folks or doing those things anymore. Most days I just sit at home in my chair with the TV on low, even though I know people are expecting me. I just can't seem to find the push to get out the door.

doctor.intent: determine the presence of psychomotor retardation
doctor.question: Do you feel like it takes you longer to do things now than it used to?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about psychomotor retardation (taking longer to do things), which is a symptom of depression or negative symptoms, but it is not specifically described in my symptom profile as a distinct manifestation of psychomotor slowing.

patient.answer:
Longer to do things? No, I wouldn't say so. When I do get around to doing something, it takes about the same amount of time it always has. Like making my tea in the afternoon. I still use the same little kettle I've had for years. It whistles when it's ready, a real sharp, high-pitched whistle. It used to drive my husband crazy, that whistle. He'd always shout from the living room for me to take it off the burner before it woke the neighbors. He worked the night shift at the plant for twenty years, so he was always trying to sleep during the day. It was terrible for his digestion, eating dinner at four in the morning. I'd make him a plate and leave it wrapped in foil in the oven to keep warm. Usually just a piece of chicken and some potatoes. We used to grow our own potatoes in the backyard. The soil back there was so rich and dark, perfect for root vegetables. You had to watch out for the potato bugs, though. Nasty little striped things that would eat all the leaves if you weren't careful. My father taught me to just pick them right off the plant and drop them in a can of soapy water. 

But... oh, my mind is wandering again, isn't it? Time. No, things don't take me any longer than they used to. Just the same as always.

doctor.question: Do you feel like your body moves more slowly than it used to when you are doing things?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about psychomotor retardation (moving more slowly), which is a symptom of depression or negative symptoms, but my Negative Symptoms profile (S023) specifically mentions avolition/apathy (lack of push/motivation) and blunted affect, not psychomotor retardation. patient.answer:
Moving slowly? No, I don't think I move any slower than I ever did. I still get around just fine. Like when I walk down to the mailbox at the end of the driveway, I just put one foot in front of the other at my usual pace. I do make sure to wear my good sturdy shoes, though. The white ones with the thick rubber soles. I bought them at that shoe store on Main Street right before it closed down. Such a shame it closed, Mr. Henderson ran that place for years and years. He had one of those heavy metal contraptions to measure your feet, you know the ones? You'd step on it and he'd slide the little metal pieces up to your toes and the side of your foot. It was always so cold on your skin if you weren't wearing thick socks. My sister Mary hated getting her feet measured. She was awfully ticklish on the bottom of her feet. If you even brushed a finger against her sole, she'd kick like a mule. We had a mule once, on my grandfather's farm when I was a little girl. Stubborn old thing named Barnaby. He wouldn't pull the plow unless my grandfather sang to him. Just old hymns, mostly. 'Rock of Ages' was Barnaby's favorite, if you can believe an animal has a favorite song... 

But... oh dear, I've lost the thread again. What did you ask me? About moving slow? No, no, I move along at a perfectly normal speed. My body does just fine.

doctor.question: Do you feel like your thoughts are moving slowly, taking longer to think through things than you used to?

patient.answer:
Thoughts moving slowly? No, I wouldn't say my thoughts are slow. They seem to move along just like they always have. I can think about things perfectly fine. Like just this morning, I was thinking about the curtains in the living room. They're a floral print, you know, with little yellow daisies and blue cornflowers. I bought that fabric at a remnant sale over at Miller's Dry Goods. Mrs. Miller was always so helpful, she'd save the best scraps for me because she knew I loved to sew. She had this big gray cat that would sleep right on the cutting table. Just a giant ball of fur, purring away while she measured out the yardage. Cats are funny creatures, aren't they? They just do exactly what they please. My neighbor, Mrs. Gable, she has three cats and they are always getting into my flowerbeds. Digging up my petunias. I tried putting chicken wire down, but they just walk right over it. Chicken wire is so sharp, you really have to be careful when you're unrolling it or it'll snap back and catch your arm. I got a nasty scratch from it once, had to put iodine on it. Iodine stings so badly, but it keeps the infection out. You always want to keep the infection out...

But... oh, what were we talking about? My thoughts? Yes, no, my thoughts are fine. They don't take any longer than they used to.

patient.answer:
Moving slowly when I get up? No, I wouldn't say so. When I get up from my chair, I just stand up and go. Like when I get up to check the mail. I have this nice wooden rocking chair by the front window. It used to belong to my grandmother, actually. The wood is so smooth on the armrests from years and years of people resting their hands there. It squeaks a little bit when you rock in it, just a tiny little creak on the left side. I tried putting some oil on the joints, but it didn't seem to help much. My husband used to use that 3-in-One oil for everything. He kept a little can of it out in the garage, right next to his toolbox. That toolbox was so heavy, made of solid steel. I tried to lift it once when we were moving and I nearly pulled my back out. You have to be careful with your back, especially as you get older. My cousin Martha slipped a disc in her back just from bending over to pick up a dropped penny at the grocery store. Can you imagine? A penny! They don't even make things you can buy for a penny anymore. When I was a girl, you could get a whole handful of Mary Janes at the corner store for a penny. The yellow wrappers with the little girl on them...

But... oh my, I'm doing it again, aren't I? Getting off track. You asked about me moving slow? No, no. When I get up and move around, I move just fine. Not slow at all.
